artworks.title: Pelops and Hippodamia
artworks.description: Kaselowsky's mural for Berlin's Neues Museum stages the chariot race that made Pelops king of Pisa: the hero and Hippodamia drive toward victory while her father Oenomaus pursues — the contest whose prize was a bride and whose aftermath named the Peloponnese. Painted in the nineteenth-century historicist idiom that lined the museum's mythological suites, the scene freezes the moment before Myrtilus's sabotage (or Poseidon's winged horses) unseats the old king. The fresco remains among the most familiar modern images of the Olympian foundation myth.

artworks.title: Terracotta plaque with Pelops and Hippodamia
artworks.description: This Augustan or Julio-Claudian terracotta plaque in the Metropolitan Museum of Art (inv. 26.60.32) shows Pelops and Hippodamia riding together in a chariot — the couple whose race against Oenomaus became the founding legend of Olympia. About 38 cm high, the Roman domestic relief translates the Greek contest into the language of Campana plaques that decorated villas and tombs. It is the portable afterlife of a story the east pediment of Zeus's temple had already carved in marble at the sanctuary itself.

artworks.title: East pediment of the Temple of Zeus at Olympia (central group)
artworks.description: In the centre of the east pediment of Zeus's temple at Olympia, Zeus stands between Oenomaus and Pelops as the rivals prepare for the chariot race that will win Hippodamia — Pausanias identifies the quiet scene as the oath before the contest, not the crash. Carved in Parian marble about 470–456 BC for the sanctuary where the games were held, the group makes Pelops the mythic founder of the Olympic contest. The sculptures are now in the Archaeological Museum of Olympia, the stone memory of the race that named the peninsula.

artworks.title: Sarcophagus of Pelops and Hippodamia
artworks.description: This Roman sarcophagus in the Tipaza Archaeological Museum, Algeria, retells Pelops' chariot race for Hippodamia in continuous relief — horses, drivers, and the bridal prize carved for a North African tomb. Imperial workshops favoured the story as an emblem of victorious love and dynastic founding. The Tipaza chest shows how far the Olympian hero travelled: from Pisa's race-track to the funerary art of the western Mediterranean.

popCulture.title: Temple of Zeus, Olympia
popCulture.description: The east pediment of Zeus's temple staged Pelops' chariot race against Oenomaus — the hero who won Hippodamia and the peninsula, carved where the games were born.

popCulture.title: Olympic Games
popCulture.description: Greek tradition tied the founding of the games at Olympia to Pelops' victory and funeral games — the hero whose race still frames the oldest athletic calendar.

popCulture.title: Peloponnese
popCulture.description: The southern peninsula kept his name: Peloponnēsos, "island of Pelops" — a geography lesson that still maps the hero onto Greece.
